turns.prompt_text: Something I would like to do is create some kind of local file. Compiler, this would primarily be for my Google Drive and Google keep And Google keep and later we would add Google images, so there would need to be some sort of Pub sub system or grab the information in batches at the end of the day or week
turns.response_html:
Building a local data pipeline for your personal Google ecosystem is a great project, especially if you want local ownership of your knowledge base or want to pipe it into a local Zettelkasten or search engine.

To handle Google Drive, Keep, and Google Photos (Images), you have a classic architectural choice to make: Batch Processing (Polling) vs. Event-Driven (Pub/Sub).

Here is a breakdown of how both approaches look for this specific ecosystem, along with a recommended hybrid architecture.

The Architectural Choice

1. The Batch Approach (Daily/Weekly Polling)

In this setup, a local script run by a scheduler (like cron or a background system daemon) wakes up, requests everything changed since the last run timestamp, processes it, and goes back to sleep.

  • Pros: Very easy to write; stateless; resilient to local network drops (it just catches up on the next run).
  • Cons: Higher latency (you have to wait for the sync interval); redundant API calls if nothing changed.

2. The Pub/Sub Approach (Real-Time Events)

In this setup, Google pushes an event to a publicly accessible endpoint (a webhook) whenever a file changes. Your local system listens for these events and processes them instantly.

  • Pros: Instantaneous; highly efficient (only runs when data changes).
  • Cons: Requires exposing a local port to the internet via a reverse proxy (like Ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnels) so Google's webhooks can find you; harder to configure.

Google Ecosystem Reality Check

The best approach actually depends on the specific Google API, because they don't all support the same features:

ServiceBest ApproachAPI Capability / Limitations
Google DriveHybrid / Pub/SubSupports Google Drive Webhooks (Watch). You can tell Google to ping a URL whenever a file or folder changes.
Google KeepStrict Batch (Third-Party)No official public API for personal accounts (the Keep API is restricted to Google Workspace enterprise domains). Real local syncing requires scraping or using unofficial Python wrappers (like gkeepapi) via batch polling.
Google PhotosStrict BatchThe Google Photos API does not support webhooks. You must poll it to check for new media items by date filters.

Recommended Architecture: The "Tracer Round" Hybrid Setup

Because of the limitations with Keep and Photos, a Robust Polling/Batch Engine with a modular ingestion pipeline is the cleanest way to start. You can build the core infrastructure first using standard batching, then easily swap the Google Drive module to real-time later if you want.

Here is a conceptual look at how to structure the local pipeline:

The Blueprint

  1. The Ingestion Layer (The "Grabbers")

    • Drive Module: Uses the official Google Drive API (pydrive2 or Google Client Libraries). It queries for files modified after last_sync_timestamp.
    • Keep Module: Uses an unofficial library or a headless browser automation script to fetch notes, converting them to local markdown or JSON files.
    • Photos Module: Uses the Google Photos API to fetch metadata and download images added after the checkpoint.

  2. The Telemetry / State Tracker

    • Keep a simple local state file (like a state.json or a lightweight SQLite DB).
    • Store a single key-value pair for each service: {"google_drive": "2026-06-19T00:00:00Z"}.
    • Every time a sync runs successfully, update this timestamp. This ensures you only request delta changes (the "diff") and don't waste bandwidth or hit API rate limits.

  3. The Orchestrator / Scheduler

    • Instead of jumping straight to a heavy message broker like RabbitMQ or Kafka, you can orchestrate this using a lightweight task framework or simple time-based execution.
    • If you are running a local terminal-centric environment or an active home server, a simple Python script kicked off by a systemd timer or a cron job running every evening is incredibly resilient and easy to debug.

Next Steps to Kick this Off

To build a quick proof-of-concept (a "tracer round" to prove the pipes work):

  1. Go to the Google Cloud Console, create a project, and enable the Drive and Photos APIs.
  2. Configure an OAuth 2.0 Desktop Application Client ID to download your local credentials file.
  3. Write a script that does nothing but successfully authenticate and print the names of the last 5 files modified in your Google Drive.

Once that connection is established, adding the local file writer and state tracking is straightforward.

Would you prefer to look at a minimal Python structural sketch for the batch orchestration script, or do you want to dive deeper into how to handle the Google Keep authentication hurdle?

turns.prompt_text: So this leads me to wonder what's the very first silver Bullet we could accomplish. Now it sounds like Drive is the easiest way to go
turns.response_html:
Starting with Google Drive is absolutely the right move. It has a fully mature, officially supported API, handles webhooks if you want to go real-time later, and lets you prove out your entire local storage and state-tracking logic without fighting authentication hurdles.

The ultimate "silver bullet"—your absolute minimal viable proof of concept (or tracer round)—is a single script that accomplishes three things:

  1. Authenticates with Google securely.
  2. Finds only the files that have changed since the last time it checked.
  3. Downloads them to a local directory.

Here is the exact blueprint to get that first wireframe up and running.

Step 1: The Google Cloud Setup

Before writing code, you need to give your local machine permission to talk to your Drive.

  1. Go to the Google Cloud Console.
  2. Create a new project (e.g., Local-File-Compiler).
  3. Enable the Google Drive API.
  4. Configure the OAuth Consent Screen as an External user type, and add your own email as a test user.
  5. Go to Credentials, click Create Credentials -> OAuth client ID, and select Desktop Application.
  6. Download the JSON file, rename it to credentials.json, and place it in your project directory.

Step 2: The Core Logic (The Script)

For a local terminal-centric environment, Python with the official google-api-python-client and google-auth-oauthlib libraries is the cleanest path.

This minimal script establishes your state tracker (using a simple local ISO timestamp) so you only fetch what's new.

import os
import datetime
from google.auth.transport.requests import Request
from google.oauth2.credentials import Credentials
from google.auth_oauthlib.flow import InstalledAppFlow
from googleapiclient.discovery import build
from googleapiclient.http import MediaIoBaseDownload

# If modifying these scopes, delete the file token.json.
SCOPES = ['https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.readonly']
STATE_FILE = "last_sync.txt"
LOCAL_TARGET_DIR = "./local_drive_sync"

def get_drive_service():
    creds = None
    if os.path.exists('token.json'):
        creds = Credentials.from_authorized_user_file('token.json', SCOPES)
    if not creds or not creds.valid:
        if creds and creds.expired and creds.refresh_token:
            creds.refresh(Request())
        else:
            flow = InstalledAppFlow.from_client_secrets_file('credentials.json', SCOPES)
            creds = flow.run_local_server(port=0)
        with open('token.json', 'w') as token:
            token.write(creds.to_json())
    return build('drive', 'v3', credentials=creds)

def get_last_sync_time():
    if os.path.exists(STATE_FILE):
        with open(STATE_FILE, 'r') as f:
            return f.read().strip()
    # Default to 24 hours ago if no state exists
    return (datetime.datetime.utcnow() - datetime.timedelta(days=1)).isoformat() + 'Z'

def update_last_sync_time(now_str):
    with open(STATE_FILE, 'w') as f:
        f.write(now_str)

def sync_changed_files():
    service = get_drive_service()
    last_sync = get_last_sync_time()
    current_run_time = datetime.datetime.utcnow().isoformat() + 'Z'
    
    print(f"Checking for files modified since: {last_sync}")
    
    # Query for files modified after last sync, excluding folders
    query = f"modifiedTime > '{last_sync}' and mimeType != 'application/vnd.google-apps.folder' and trashed = false"
    
    results = service.files().list(
        q=query,
        fields="nextPageToken, files(id, name, modifiedTime, mimeType)",
        pageSize=10
    ).execute()
    
    files = results.get('files', [])
    
    if not files:
        print("Everything is up to date.")
        update_last_sync_time(current_run_time)
        return

    os.makedirs(LOCAL_TARGET_DIR, exist_ok=True)

    for file in files:
        file_id = file['id']
        file_name = file['name']
        print(f"Found modified file: {file_name} (ID: {file_id})")
        
        # Note: Google Docs/Sheets require exporting, binary files can be downloaded directly
        if "vnd.google-apps" in file['mimeType']:
            print(f"-> Skipping Google Workspace doc '{file_name}' (requires export conversion).")
            continue
            
        # Download binary file (PDFs, Markdown, text, etc.)
        request = service.files().get_media(fileId=file_id)
        local_path = os.path.join(LOCAL_TARGET_DIR, file_name)
        
        with open(local_path, 'wb') as f:
            downloader = MediaIoBaseDownload(f, request)
            done = False
            while not done:
                status, done = downloader.next_chunk()
        print(f"-> Successfully downloaded to {local_path}")

    # Update state only after a successful loop
    update_last_sync_time(current_run_time)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    sync_changed_files()

Step 3: Why This works as the Foundation

By setting it up this way, you've solved the hardest architectural patterns on day one:

  1. The Token Lifecycle: token.json saves your login so this can run headless later (via a cron job or systemd timer) without prompting you for a browser login every time.
  2. The Deltas (The Diff): By relying on modifiedTime > last_sync, you ensure that whether you run this every 5 minutes or once a week, it only grabs what it needs.
  3. The Local Mirror: It creates a predictable sandbox folder (./local_drive_sync) where you can later point parsing engines (like an Obsidian Vault indexer or markdown compiler).

Once you run this manually in your terminal and see a file pull down locally based on a timestamp change, your infrastructure pipe is verified. From there, we can look at handling native Google Doc formats (which require an explicit .export() call to convert them to Markdown or PDF) or start tackling the Keep scraping layer.

turns.prompt_text: So I actually have a drive folder on my computer, however I don't know if they actually cache it locally or if they still have to redownload it like how it works with iCloud
turns.response_html:
This is the exact right question to ask because it completely changes how you build your compiler.

By default, Google Drive for Desktop behaves exactly like iCloud. It uses a method called "Streaming", which means your local folder is actually a phantom "virtual drive." The files look like they are there, but they are just placeholders. The moment your compiler script tries to read a file, Google Drive hurriedly downloads it in the background to a temporary local cache.

However, Google Drive has a major advantage over iCloud: you can easily force it to store everything physically on your machine.

The Solution: Switch to "Mirroring"

If you want your files to sit permanently on your hard drive so your compiler can instantly read them without hitting the internet, you can toggle a single setting in the app.

How to turn on Mirroring:

  1. Click the Google Drive icon in your system tray (Windows) or menu bar (Mac).
  2. Click the Gear icon and select Preferences.
  3. On the left sidebar, click Google Drive (Folders from Drive).
  4. Under "My Drive syncing options," switch from Stream files to Mirror files.
[ Stream files ] -> Cloud-only placeholders (downloads on-demand)
[ Mirror files ] -> True 1-to-1 local copy (stored permanently on disk)

Warning on Google Docs/Sheets: Even with "Mirroring" turned on, native Google formats (like .gdoc or .gsheet) will still just download as tiny 1 KB shortcut links that point to the web browser. If your local file compiler needs to read raw text from Docs, you will still need to use the Python script method we discussed earlier to explicitly .export() them into standard Markdown or Text formats.

How this changes your local compiler plan

If you turn on Mirroring, your entire pipeline gets 90% simpler. You don't even need the Google API script anymore.

Your "Silver Bullet" shifts from an API project to a simple local file watcher:

  1. Google Drive handles all the background downloading and sync state natively.
  2. Your local compiler script simply watches your local mirrored folder (e.g., C:\Users\You\Google Drive\My Drive) for new changes.
  3. Your script compiles them locally on your machine, 100% offline.

If you go this route, your next step would simply be writing a script to look through that folder, find your text files, and parse them. Would you rather stick to the API route (which keeps your hard drive clean), or switch to Mirroring and build a script that reads straight from your local file explorer?

turns.prompt_text: So I will not turn on mirroring to save my storage space. But I'm okay if the script is a little slower because it has to wait for a download as long as it's robust
turns.response_html:
Smart move. Keeping it on "Streaming" saves your local drive from bloating, and since we are planning for a batch or pub/sub system that runs in the background anyway, speed isn't our bottleneck—robustness is.

Since you are sticking with the streaming file structure, you have two distinct paths for your script to get the actual file data. Here is how they compare for robustness:

Path A: The Direct API Route (Recommended)

This bypasses your desktop app completely. Your script talks directly to Google's cloud servers via the API code we looked at earlier.

  • Why it's robust: It doesn't care if your desktop Google Drive app is running, crashed, or paused. It pulls the data straight from the source.
  • How it handles streaming: It downloads the file directly into a dedicated local cache folder (./local_drive_sync) only when the script runs, and you can delete it whenever you want to free up space.

Path B: The Local File-System Poke

Your script looks at the virtual streaming folder on your computer (e.g., /Volumes/GoogleDrive/My Drive/ on macOS).

  • Why it's risky: When a script tries to read a streamed file, it triggers the Google Drive desktop app to quickly fetch it. If the app is glitching, if your network drops mid-read, or if you try to read a 50MB file before the desktop app finishes downloading it, your script will crash with an IOError or read a corrupted, half-empty file.
  • How it handles streaming: It forces the desktop app to download the file into its hidden system cache, meaning you are still technically using up local storage space behind the scenes until the app decides to purge it.

Designing for Bulletproof Robustness (Path A)

If we go with the Direct API Route, we can build in specific "defensive driving" features to handle the slow downloads and network drops elegantly:

  1. The Checkpoint File: The script updates its last_sync.txt timestamp only after a file successfully downloads. If the internet cuts out on file 4 of 10, the script crashes safely, and the next time it runs, it picks up right at file 4.
  2. Auto-Exporting Google Docs: If you have native Google Docs, the API allows us to convert them on-the-fly to plain text or Markdown during the download, meaning your compiler gets clean text without any placeholder link junk.
  3. Explicit Timeout Handling: We can wrap the download worker in a standard retry loop. If Google's servers take too long to respond, it waits 5 seconds and tries again.

You can breathe a sigh of relief: you won't be paying a dime. For a single-user personal project like this, it is practically impossible to trigger any costs. Google handles API billing differently than standard cloud compute infrastructure (like AWS EC2 or Google Cloud VMs). Here is why you are completely safe.

1. No Compute is Happening in the Cloud

When you run a Python sync script on your local machine, your computer is doing 100% of the work.

  • Google isn't spinning up virtual machines or allocating server memory for you.
  • You are simply asking Google's database for file metadata and downloading the bytes.

Because you aren't using Google's cloud servers to execute code, there are no compute costs.

2. Google Workspace API Quotas Are Massive (and Free)

Google gives every developer project a free, standard tier of daily API requests to prevent abuse. For personal data harvesting, the limits are astronomically higher than you will ever need:

  • The Quota: The standard Drive API limit allows up to 1,000,000 quota units per minute and up to 1 TB of data transfer per day per project.
  • Your Scaling Reality: A daily batch script that checks for changed files and downloads a few PDFs or text files uses maybe 10 to 50 requests total. Even if you modified thousands of files a day, you wouldn't even scratch 1% of the free per-minute limit.

While Google has announced plans to introduce charges for enterprise developers who completely blow past these massive caps later in 2026, standard usage remains entirely free of charge.

3. How to Protect Yourself Anyway (The Hard Cap)

If you are still nervous about a rogue while True: loop in your code accidentally firing off millions of requests while you're asleep, you can set an ironclad safety net in the Google Cloud Console.

You can explicitly cap your project's maximum allowed daily API usage:

  1. In the Google Cloud Console, go to APIs & Services -> Dashboard.
  2. Click on the Google Drive API.
  3. Navigate to the Quotas tab.
  4. Manually edit the Queries per day and smash it down to something like 5,000.

If your script ever goes crazy, Google will instantly block it with a 429 Too Many Requests error, protecting your account before it ever becomes an issue.

You don't even need to link a credit card or set up a billing profile to get started with the Desktop Client credentials. It is entirely sandboxed and safe. Knowing it's completely free to build, should we look at how to structure that initial credentials.json login flow?

turns.prompt_text: So I have another question. Eventually I will want to download all of my Google images Is there any way to do that? I would prefer to do it in chunks or batches as there's potentially a massive amount of I believe 100 GB Which is technically not that massive, but it's a lot more than I've normally dealt with
turns.response_html:
Yes, there is absolutely a way to do this, and you are 100% right to want to batch it. Trying to pull down 100 GB of images in one massive, uninterrupted dump is asking for a connection timeout, a corrupted file, or an accidental API ban.

When you scale up to pulling your Google Photos library into your local compiler, you have two entirely different ways to attack it.

Option A: The One-Time "Brute Force" Catchup (Google Takeout)

Before you even write a line of photo-downloading code, you should look at Google Takeout (takeout.google.com).

  • How it works: You log in, select only Google Photos, and tell Google to package your entire 100 GB library into manageable chunks (e.g., twenty 5 GB .zip files). Google compresses it all on their servers and emails you download links when it's ready.
  • Why it's great: It saves you thousands of API calls, downloads incredibly fast, and gets your initial historical 100 GB baseline sitting on your computer in an afternoon.
  • The Catch: It strips out some of your photo metadata (like the exact GPS coordinates or dates you edited) and shoves that metadata into separate, messy .json files next to the images. If your compiler is highly dependent on photo dates, you have to write code to parse those sidecar JSON files.

Option B: The Automated API Script (The Long-Game Approach)

If you want clean images with their original metadata untouched, you can write a loop into your compiler using the Google Photos API.

Because 100 GB is a lot of data transfer, you must structure the loop defensively to chunk the downloads safely. Here is how you handle the math and logic:

  1. The Daily Quota Buffer: Google allows a single developer project to access up to 75,000 "media bytes" requests per day for free. One photo download = 1 request. If your average photo/video size is 4MB, you could theoretically download up to 300 GB a day for free, but you don't want to push it.
  2. Chunking by Date or Batch Size: The Photos API lets you query media in batches of up to 100 items per page. Your code will pull a list of 100 images, download them one by one to your local directory, update its progress state, and then grab the next page using a nextPageToken.
  3. The "Resume" Checkpoint: Because network drops will happen over 100 GB, you don't track your state by a simple timestamp like you do with Drive. Instead, you keep a local ledger (a mini SQLite database or text file) of every unique Photo_ID you've already successfully downloaded. If the script crashes after downloading 12 GB, you run it again, and it instantly skips those 12 GB of IDs and moves to the next batch.

The Recommended Playbook

The most robust strategy is a combination of both:

  1. Day 1: Kick off a Google Takeout to grab the massive bulk 100 GB chunk. Dump all those files into your local media folder.
  2. Day 2: Hook up your Python compiler to the Google Photos API, but write your query to only look for photos added in the last 7 days.

This prevents you from having to download 100 GB over an API connection. Your code stays incredibly lightweight, it only has to worry about a few hundred megabytes of new photos a week, and your network remains completely happy.

When you're ready to add the image layer, we can easily plug that date-filtered Photos loop straight into the main Drive orchestrator script we sketched out!

turns.prompt_text: So I have a problem with Google takeout and that I've never gotten it to work. It always fails. I wonder how I can make it run more safely
turns.response_html:
That is an incredibly common frustration. The secret reason Google Takeout constantly fails—especially on large accounts like your 100 GB library—is because of how Google handles it under the hood.

Takeout tries to bundle tens of thousands of files across different Google services all at once. If a single corporate team's database times out, or if you have a couple of corrupted video files, or if your internet drops for a fraction of a second during a massive multi-gigabyte download, the entire process breaks and gives you a generic "Something went wrong" error.

To make Google Takeout run reliably, you have to strip away its complexity. Here is the checklist to force it to succeed:

1. Isolate the Service (One Product at a Time)

When you go to takeout.google.com, the very first thing you should do is click Deselect All.

  • Never try to export "All Google Data" at once.
  • Create one separate export request just for Google Photos.
  • If you want your Drive data, handle that as a completely separate request later. This prevents a failure in one service from ruining the download for another.

2. Drop the Archive Size to 2 GB or 5 GB

By default, Google sets the archive split size to 50 GB. For a 100 GB library, that means Google tries to create two massive 50 GB zip files.

  • If your home internet connection has even a tiny hiccup while downloading a 50 GB file, the download fails, cannot be resumed, and you have to start over.
  • The Fix: Change the archive size dropdown to 2 GB or 5 GB.
  • This tells Google to split your 100 GB library into 20 to 50 small zip files. Small files download fast, don't time out, and if one single zip fails, you only have to re-download that specific 2 GB chunk instead of losing the whole progress.

3. Don't Export Every Single Album

Inside the Google Photos section on the Takeout page, click the button that says All photo albums included.

  • Uncheck old, giant auto-generated folders you don't care about (like "Photos from 2012" if you've already backed them up elsewhere).
  • If you have a particularly massive year or album that you suspect is causing the crash, uncheck it and export it by itself.

4. Run it in a Clean Browser Environment

Browser extensions (especially heavy ad-blockers, privacy wrappers, or download managers) can aggressively block the background scripts Google Takeout uses to stitch your archives together.

  • Log into an Incognito / Private window with all extensions disabled when you kick off the export and when you download the finished zip links.

🛠️ The "Post-Takeout" Missing Metadata Trick

When you finally get those zip files down, you're going to notice a weird glitch: your photos will lose their original "Date Taken" and GPS coordinates in your file explorer, and Google will stick that data into annoying .json sidecar files right next to the images.

Don't panic or try to fix it manually. The open-source community built a bulletproof, free tool specifically for this called Google Photos Takeout Helper. It's a simple script that reads those JSON files, stamps the metadata back into the actual images, and cleans up the mess for you.

If you break your library into small 2 GB chunks and run it isolated, Takeout should finally behave. Do you want to try kicking off a small 2 GB test export for just a single year of photos to see if it makes it through the pipeline?

turns.prompt_text: So I imagine the best way to do this actually would just be to go to Google photos and chunkize the photos and download them as archives. Or if there's a compressed format, do that
turns.response_html:
You hit the nail on the head. If you bypass the automated Google Takeout wizard entirely and instead log into the standard Google Photos web interface on a computer, you can manually "chunkize" your library by selecting chunks of images and hitting Shift + D to download them as immediate zip files.

This approach completely circumvents the waiting time, server-side failures, and processing lag of Google Takeout.

If you choose this manual chunking route, keep these operational boundaries in mind:

1. The 500-Item Limit Rule

Google Photos has a hard limit when downloading directly from the web interface: you can only download up to 500 items at a time in a single selection.

  • If you select 501 photos, the "Download" option disappears or throws an error.
  • The Strategy: The easiest way to select a clean chunk is to leverage the timeline view. Click the checkmark on a specific date header (e.g., "October 14, 2025") to select the whole day. Hold Shift and click a date header from a few weeks prior until your selected count in the top-left corner sits right under 500. Then click the three dots in the top right and hit Download.

2. The Native Compression Multiplier

When you download images this way, Google automatically compresses them into a single .zip archive on the fly.

  • Because you kept the chunk under 500 items, the zip file size will usually hover between 1 GB and 3 GB (depending on how much 4K video you shot in that window).
  • These bite-sized archives are highly stable to download, completely bypassing the network timeout issues that plague giant downloads.

3. The Metadata Victory 🏆

Here is the biggest reason to use this method over Google Takeout: it preserves your image metadata.

  • When you download directly from the web layout, Google keeps the original EXIF metadata (the exact camera settings, GPS coordinates, and the exact timestamp the shutter clicked) embedded right inside the JPEG/RAW headers.
  • You won't have to deal with thousands of loose, messy .json sidecar files or use a helper script to re-stitch your files back together. They are ready for your local compiler immediately upon unzipping.

The Workflow Setup

To execute this cleanly without losing track of your progress over a 100 GB library:

  1. Create a dedicated folder on your computer called /local_media_sink/raw_zips/.
  2. Start from the present day in your browser and select your first chunk of ~450 files. Download it, and immediately rename the resulting zip file to something sequential, like 001_June2026.zip.
  3. Scroll down to where you left off, select the next chunk moving backward in time, and name it 002_Spring2026.zip.
  4. Once you have a handful of zips, you can use a quick bash loop or a Python snippet in your local terminal to unzip them all into a structured asset directory in one go:
for file in *.zip; do unzip "$file" -d "../unzipped_photos/"; done

By manually orchestrating the chunks in 500-item blocks, you match the speed of your network, preserve the structural integrity of your images, and completely eliminate cloud execution errors.

turns.prompt_text: I have 6050 photos, 22.5 GB of space
turns.response_html:
6,050 photos and 22.5 GB of data is the absolute sweet spot for a manual chunking strategy. It’s small enough that you can knock it out in about 15 to 20 minutes at your desk, but large enough that a standard web browser would choke if you tried to download it all in one click.

Because we want to bypass the unreliable Takeout engine entirely while preserving all your original metadata, here is how you math out the chunking strategy and execute it flawlessly.

The Download Blueprint (The Math)

Google's web interface has a strict single-download selection cap of 500 items. If you try to pull 501, the web engine will fail.

To download 6,050 photos, you need to break the project down into exactly 13 chunks (averaging roughly ~460 photos per chunk).

  • Photos per zip file: ~460 items
  • Estimated size per zip file: ~1.7 GB (Highly stable for any modern internet connection)
  • Total archives to download: 13 files

Step-by-Step Execution Plan

1. Preparation

Create a landing zone on your machine. Do not dump these files into your standard Downloads folder. Create a dedicated workspace folder, like: ~/google_photos_sync/archives/.

2. The Selection Dance

  1. Open Google Photos in a desktop browser and go to your main timeline view (photos.google.com).
  2. Hover over the very first photo at the top of your feed and click the small checkmark in its top-left corner.
  3. Scroll down the page. (Don't speed-scroll to the bottom; let the page render the thumbnails as you pass them so the browser registers them).
  4. Look at the selection counter in the top-left blue bar of your browser window. Once you have scrolled down roughly 5 or 6 months (or what looks like a few hundred photos), hold the Shift key and click the checkmark on a photo.
  5. Look at the blue counter.
    • If it's under 500: Excellent.
    • If it's over 500: Keep holding Shift and click a photo slightly higher up until the counter drops back into the safe zone (e.g., 450).

3. Triggering the Archive

With your ~450 files highlighted, press Shift + D on your keyboard (or click the three dots in the top right and select Download).

Google will immediately show a quick "Zipping..." status bar at the bottom left of your screen. Within a minute, a crisp 1.5 GB zip file will download to your machine.

4. Tagging the Progress

As soon as the download finishes, go to your terminal or file explorer and rename that file immediately to prevent losing your place. Use a structured, sequential index:

  • 001_recent.zip
  • 002_early2026.zip
  • 003_late2025.zip

Go back to the browser window, hit the X in the top left of the blue bar to clear your current selection, and repeat the process starting exactly where you left off.

Automating the Local Extraction

Once you have your 13 zip files resting safely in your folder, you don't want to double-click all of them manually. You can extract them all natively via your terminal in seconds.

Navigate to your workspace directory and execute a quick compression loop to unpack the entire 22.5 GB library cleanly into an asset folder:

mkdir -p ../unpacked_photos && for file in *.zip; do unzip "$file" -d "../unpacked_photos/"; done

Because you grabbed them natively from the web app, your files are instantly ready for your local compiler pipeline. Every single image will contain its original embedded camera coordinates, lens specs, and creation timestamps, with zero annoying .json sidecar files to parse.
